strengths: The paper offers a genuinely new perspective on KV cache eviction by formalizing 'criticality' as minimization of attention output perturbation (Definition 3.1), moving beyond the purely empirical attention-weight heuristics used in prior work (H2O, SnapKV, AdaKV). The key insight—that projected value states ||V_i W^O||_1 matter in addition to attention weights—is well-motivated by the derivation in Theorem 3.3.

The theoretical treatment is clean and mostly correct. Theorem 3.2 correctly relates masked and unmasked attention via a multiplicative mask; Theorem 3.3 derives a per-entry-decomposable upper bound on the L1 perturbation; Theorem 3.5 shows the two-stage greedy algorithm minimizes a valid (conditional) upper bound. Notably, Theorem E.1 in the appendix elegantly shows that prior attention-only selection is equivalent to minimizing a looser, relaxed bound, which neatly explains why the proposed method can outperform it.

The method is a drop-in replacement for the Top-K selection step of existing SOTA evictors (SnapKV, AdaKV), making it practical and easily integrable; the experimental design compares w/ vs. w/o the algorithm under identical settings, which isolates the contribution.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: two models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), two compression scenarios (regular and the more challenging context-only), two budgets, Needle-in-a-Haystack (single/multi retrieval) and 16 LongBench datasets across six domains, plus mechanism-level validation (head-wise/layer-wise/budget-wise perturbation reductions, and appendix validation of Assumption 3.4 in >99% of heads). Gains are consistent, e.g., multi-retrieval improvement from 60.5 to 91.25 and LongBench improvements in 19-24 of 24 domain-settings.

The paper is fairly honest about limitations of the assumption (Appendix A acknowledges first-layer heads violating Assumption 3.4 and analyzes the impact), and includes ablations on the distance metric (L1 vs L2, Appendix F).
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency on the hyperparameter: Algorithm 1 (page 4) states 'Hyper Parameter α = 0.25', while Section 3.5 states α is fixed at 0.5, and Section 4.3 says α = 0.5 'for all experiments'. This inconsistency between the algorithm specification and the evaluated configuration undermines reproducibility and suggests insufficient proofreading.

The theory is looser than the framing suggests. The upper bound uses the triangle inequality and split per-index absolute values; minimizing the bound (and a conditional bound θ̂ under Assumption 3.4) does not provably minimize the actual perturbation, and the paper itself concedes no strict improvement is guaranteed (Appendix E). Moreover, the analysis is derived for a single query/single token, while the practical algorithm operates on attention accumulated over an observation window with pooling (Algorithm 2); the transfer of the theory to this accumulated setting is heuristic and not formally justified.

No overhead analysis despite the method requiring the L1 norms of value states projected through W^O (which must be computed or cached for all n entries, per head). For an efficiency-focused paper, the missing wall-clock/latency/memory overhead comparison against the base methods is a significant omission. Relatedly, the formulation treats W^O as a per-head d_h × d matrix (Eq. 2), whereas in standard multi-head attention the output projection acts on concatenated heads; this architectural simplification is not acknowledged.

Baselines are narrow: only SnapKV, AdaKV, and StreamingLLM are compared, with the contribution demonstrated solely as an add-on. No comparison against other recent evictors (e.g., PyramidKV, Quest-style or GQA-aware variants) or against alternative perturbation/sensitivity-based selection strategies, so it is hard to gauge how the criterion compares to other non-attention-weight signals.

Evaluation concerns: NIAH results use only 100 samples with no variance/significance reporting; gains in the regular-compression LongBench setting are small (often <0.5 points); only two ~7-8B models are tested, leaving generality (larger models, other families, GQA configurations) unverified. No code or artifact release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

Presentation has notable flaws: the running title is broken ('Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size') on every page; Figure 5/9 captions reference tokens inconsistently with the text (text reports tokens 1, 2, 3; captions say Token1/Token3/Token5); the notation 'A' (bold) is silently redefined in Algorithm 1 as A_i||V_i,:||_1, which is confusing; several typos ('incorperated', 'quantifies'); and Table 1's '6711' column label is cryptic. The main text also asserts 'lower output perturbations in over 92% attention heads' as a headline claim without statistical treatment.

The claimed significance is moderate: the empirical contribution is an incremental improvement to existing evictors, and the theoretical contribution, while neat, is a bound-driven heuristic (two-stage Top-K) rather than an algorithm with optimality guarantees; the gap between 'constraining worst-case perturbation' rhetoric and what is actually guaranteed (minimizing a loose, conditional surrogate) slightly overstates the rigor.

strengths: The paper formalizes cache entry criticality via output perturbation (Definition 3.1), giving a principled reframing of what has been a purely heuristic attention-weight-based selection problem in KV cache eviction.

Theorem 3.3 and the derivation in Section 3.3 are correct as far as they go, and the observation that projected value states ||Vi WO||1 matter in addition to attention weights is a reasonable and useful insight; Theorem E.1 in the appendix neatly explains prior attention-only selection as minimizing a relaxed bound.
The proposed algorithm is simple and integrates cleanly into existing methods (SnapKV, AdaKV) without changing their accumulation machinery, which makes adoption easy.

The evaluation is fairly broad in coverage: two compression scenarios (regular and the more realistic context-only setting), Needle-in-a-Haystack (single and multi retrieval), and 16 LongBench datasets, plus head-wise/layer-wise/budget-wise perturbation analyses and appendix validation of the key assumption (Figure 8).
The context-only compression results show substantial, practically relevant gains (e.g., multi-retrieval from 21.75 to 96 for Mistral at 40% cache size).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is weaker than advertised. The 'worst-case perturbation' bound is a straightforward triangle-inequality relaxation, and the greedy two-stage algorithm does not actually optimize the stated bound in general: stage 1 fixes sigma before stage 2, and the reduction of minimizing theta-hat to a Top-K on Ai*||Vi,:||1 holds only under Assumption 3.4, an empirical assumption that the paper itself acknowledges fails for first-layer heads. The claim of a 'formal' / 'theoretical' framework oversells what is essentially a heuristic justified by a loose bound.

A significant conceptual gap: the perturbation analysis conditions on the current query q (from the observation window), but eviction happens once at prefill time while future decoding queries differ. The bound therefore does not apply to the queries actually encountered during generation, and this mismatch is not analyzed or even discussed.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence: Algorithm 1 states a hyperparameter alpha = 0.25, while the Assumption 3.4 discussion and Section 4.3 say alpha is set to 0.5 for all experiments. The running title is broken ('Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size') across the whole manuscript, and several sentences contain grammatical errors, suggesting insufficient care in preparation.

The empirical evaluation is limited on the model axis (only Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B), reports no variance, seeds, or significance testing, and the headline comparisons are only 'method w/ ours vs. w/o ours' plus a weak StreamingLLM reference; no comparison against other recent eviction or value-aware baselines (e.g., PyramidKV, Quest, or value-norm-aware variants) is provided to establish state-of-the-art claims.

No efficiency analysis is given despite the motivation being inference cost: computing Ai*||Vi,:||1 requires projecting all cached values through WO and computing norms, which adds memory traffic and compute; whether the quality gains justify this overhead is never quantified (no throughput, latency, or wall-clock numbers).

Gains in the regular compression scenario are small (often <1 point on LongBench averages, e.g., 48.29 vs 48.73 at 20% SnapKV), and the large gains concentrate in the context-only setting at small budgets; the paper does not discuss when the method helps little or hurts (e.g., some Summarization and Multi-Doc entries in Table 1 decrease).

The argument that optimizing a tighter bound 'often achieves better results' (Appendix E) is informal; there is no guarantee or empirical characterization of when the tighter bound yields better selections, and no ablation isolating the contribution of the two-stage design versus simply ranking by Ai*||Vi||1 for the whole budget.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters and templates are documented, but no code release is mentioned, and details needed to replicate the perturbation-tracking experiments (Section 4.6) are thin.

strengths: The paper formalizes cache entry criticality via output perturbation (Def. 3.1) rather than relying on purely empirical attention heuristics, which is a genuinely useful reframing of the eviction problem.

The derivation of the perturbation upper bound (Theorems 3.3 and 3.5) is correct as far as I can verify: the L1 bound decomposes into attention weights times L1 norms of value states projected through W^O, and the two-stage decomposition in Theorem 3.5 validly reduces stage 2 to a linear objective solvable exactly by Top-K on A_i * ||V_i,:||_1.

Theorem E.1 is a nice addition: it shows prior attention-only selection is equivalent to minimizing a strictly looser upper bound, which both explains prior methods and justifies the new criterion within a single framework.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: two models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B), Needle-in-a-Haystack (single and multi retrieval), LongBench across 16 datasets in six domains, two cache sizes, and two compression scenarios including the harder and more realistic context-only setting, where the gains are substantial (e.g., multi-retrieval 60.5 -> 91.25 for Llama at 20% cache with AdaKV).
The method is a drop-in replacement for the selection step of SnapKV/AdaKV (Algorithm 2), making it easy to adopt and easy to compare against the base methods it improves.

The analysis section (head-wise, layer-wise, budget-wise perturbation) ties the theoretical criterion to observed quality improvements, and Appendix A honestly reports where Assumption 3.4 fails (first-layer heads) and quantifies the impact (<1% of heads).
weaknesses: No evaluation of computational or memory overhead. The selection step requires computing V_i * W^O (i.e., projected value states through the output matrix) for all n entries per head, which is the same order of cost as computing the attention output itself. For a paper about efficient inference, the absence of wall-clock latency, prefill overhead, or memory measurements is a significant omission that undermines the practical significance of the gains.

The theory-to-algorithm gap is acknowledged but not fully resolved: the method minimizes upper bounds (theta-hat bounds theta bounds L), so lower worst-case bound does not guarantee lower actual perturbation; empirically ~8% of heads still show higher perturbation (Figure 5). The main-text framing ('directly constrains the worst-case output perturbation') overstates what is guaranteed.

Internal inconsistency on the hyperparameter alpha: Algorithm 1 states alpha = 0.25, while Section 3.5 and Section 4.3 state alpha = 0.5. This must be corrected, and there is no ablation over alpha values in the main text.

The perturbation analysis is formulated for a single query, but in the observation-window pipeline (Algorithm 2) the selection uses mean-pooled, max-pooled accumulated attention. The extension of the worst-case bound to pooled attention scores is heuristic and not formalized, even though this is the configuration used in the headline experiments.

Only two ~7-8B open-weight models are evaluated; no smaller/larger models, no GQA-specific discussion of how per-head budget interacts with grouped KV storage (relevant for AdaKV-style head-wise budgets), and no statistical significance or variance reporting for NIAH (100 samples).

The claim of being the 'first analysis of output perturbations' for cache eviction should be tempered; value-state magnitudes have appeared in heuristic form in adjacent pruning/eviction literature, and the related-work discussion of value-aware selection could be more thorough.

Presentation issues: repeated placeholder running title ('Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size') on every page, several figures with unreadable axis labels and legend/axis mismatches (Figures 3, 4, 8), and minor writing errors (e.g., 'incorperated', eq. 11 notation for the normalization term).
Impact Statement is boilerplate; there is no explicit limitations section in the main paper, although some limitations are discussed in Appendix A.
